html:
Navarre was a small Christian kingdom in the western Pyrenees, with its capital at Pamplona, from the 800s until it was split between Spain and France. On the map it appears from 1000 to 1500, squeezed between Castile, Aragon and France.

It began around 824 as the Kingdom of Pamplona, under the Basque chief Íñigo Arista, in lands of the Basques that neither the Franks nor the Muslims of al-Andalus fully controlled. Its great moment came under Sancho III, called the Great, who by his death in 1035 ruled or dominated most of Christian Spain. He split his lands among his sons, and two of the pieces became the kingdoms of Castile and Aragon.

After that Navarre was boxed in. It could not take part in the Reconquista's push south, so it turned north:

  • The pilgrim road of the Camino de Santiago crossed it at Roncesvalles and Pamplona and brought trade.
  • From 1234 French noble houses held the crown, and from 1284 to 1328 the kings of France were also kings of Navarre.
  • Its towns and nobles kept strong local laws, the fueros.

In 1512 Ferdinand II of Aragon conquered the part south of the Pyrenees, which was joined to Castile and so to Spain. The small northern part lived on as a kingdom. Its king became Henry IV of France in 1589, and in 1620 it was merged into France.
sum: Navarre was a small Christian kingdom in the western Pyrenees, with its capital at Pamplona, from the 800s until it was split between Spain and France. On the map it appears from 1000 to 1500, squeezed between Castile, Aragon and France.
